title: Augustine (354–430)
hook: a brilliant, restless young man hears a child singing take and read and opens the Bible

segments.voice: Yesterday, intercession: why Catholics ask Mary, and friends, to pray for them. Your line was pray for us. Did you ask someone? Day eighty-five. A new week: the saints, one by one.

He's thirty-one. He's one of the most brilliant speakers in the Roman Empire, teaching in the emperor's city of Milan. He has a career, admirers, a partner of many years, a teenage son. And he is miserable. For more than a decade he's been searching: philosophy, a strange religion that promised secret knowledge, ambition, pleasure. His mother, Monica, has prayed for him every day of his adult life. He knows, by now, that he wants to follow Christ. He just can't make himself do it. Years later he wrote down the prayer he prayed back then, and it's painfully honest. In Pusey's translation: "Give me chastity and continency, only not yet." Today: the saint who said not yet.
screen: `BRILLIANT, SUCCESSFUL, MISERABLE.` → `A MOTHER WHO PRAYED.` → `ONLY NOT YET.`

segments.voice: Augustine was born in North Africa, in what's now Algeria, in the year 354. His book the Confessions, written as one long prayer to God, is often called the first real autobiography. And the turning point is in a garden in Milan. He's sitting under a fig tree, weeping, sick of himself. Then from a house nearby he hears a child's voice, singing something like a game, over and over. In Pusey's translation: "Take up and read; Take up and read." He can't think of any children's game with those words. So he takes it as a sign, goes back to where he'd left a book of Paul's letters, opens it, and reads the first thing his eyes fall on. It's from Romans: not in partying and drunkenness, not in sleeping around, not in fighting and envy, "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He says a light flooded his heart and the doubt just went. He was baptized that Easter by Ambrose, the bishop of Milan. Monica saw it before she died. He went on to be a bishop in North Africa for thirty-five years, and his writing shaped Western Christianity more than almost anyone's after Paul. The Church calls him a Doctor of the Church. But most people remember one line, from the very first page of the Confessions: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The restlessness, Augustine says, isn't a flaw. It's a compass.
screen: `NORTH AFRICA, 354.` · `A CHILD SINGS: TAKE UP AND READ.` · `PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.` · `RESTLESSNESS AS A COMPASS.` · then, large: `OUR HEART IS RESTLESS, UNTIL IT REPOSE IN THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take up and read. If there's a Bible near you, or one on your phone, open it anywhere and read one verse. Just one. If there isn't, bring to mind any line of Scripture you already know. Then settle and breathe, and let it sit. Don't analyze it. Notice if anything in it catches. Catholics don't treat this as fortune-telling, and Augustine didn't either. It's just letting a word find you. If you pray, you can ask what it's saying to you today. The bell holds the time.
Augustine. The restless, brilliant North African who heard a child sing take up and read, and became one of the Church's great teachers. Today's word.
Your line: our heart is restless. Today, when you feel restless, don't just scroll it away. Ask what it's looking for. Day eighty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Augustine on 28 August, the day after his mother Saint Monica, and many read his Confessions as a classic of prayer.

original.note: Latin: take up and read. the words Augustine heard sung in the garden in Milan.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old saint who wrote hard books.
what it means: a brilliant, restless man, prayed for by his mother, who heard a child sing and finally said yes.
what a scholar hears: tolle lege, Confessions book eight. and the first page, fecisti nos ad te, you made us for yourself, is one of the most quoted lines in Christian writing.

notes: Pusey (1838) wording of Confessions 1.1, 8.7 and 8.12 given from memory; confirm exact words ('continency', capitalized 'Thee/Thyself').
Romans 13:13 is paraphrased in modern words ('partying... sleeping around') rather than quoted; Keeper may prefer the Douay-Rheims wording. Romans 13:14 quoted from the Douay-Rheims; confirm.
Dates: born 13 November 354 at Thagaste; conversion 386 in Milan, age 31/32; baptized by Ambrose at Easter 387; bishop of Hippo c. 395/396–430 (about 35 years); died 430. Confirm.
'A strange religion that promised secret knowledge' refers to Manichaeism; confirm the description is fair.
The practice notes Catholics don't treat random Bible-opening as fortune-telling (Augustine himself warned against sortes); confirm phrasing.
